job.system:
You are the AI assistant for the Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: The Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining (CADM) is a nonprofit advocacy organization based in Washington, DC. We believe that the industrial mining of the deep seabed, meaning the large-scale extraction of minerals from the ocean floor, poses a serious risk of irreversible destruction to deep-ocean ecosystems, and that no one currently knows how to conduct it without such damage. Our goal is a legally binding prohibition on commercial deep-sea mining, first in the United States and then through an international treaty. We work through lobbying, grassroots organizing, and public education.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which we strongly support. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
Here's a section-by-section review of S. 2817 as amended. I've ordered the issues by section; a short "worst five" note follows at the end to help with prioritizing amendments for the 15th.

**Sec. 2(1)(A) – Definition of "commercial deep seabed mining"**

1. **Sec. 2(1)(A) – "by a single vessel."** The 10,000-ton threshold is measured per vessel, so an operator can split production across several vessels (or affiliated shell companies) that each stay under the cap. There is no aggregation rule for fleets, affiliates, or contractors working the same license area.

2. **Sec. 2(1)(A) – "per year."** The bill does not say whether "year" means calendar year, fiscal year, or any rolling 12-month period, nor who measures it or how (wet vs. dry weight, nodules only vs. nodules plus sediment). An operator can time campaigns across a year boundary to stay under the threshold in each.

3. **Sec. 2(1)(A) – 10,000-ton threshold is arbitrary and high.** Collector-system trials and pilot mining — which is exactly what the industry is doing now, and which already causes documented plume and benthic damage — can fall well below 10,000 tons. Seafloor massive sulfide and cobalt-crust mining are lower-volume by nature and could be effectively unregulated.

4. **Sec. 2(1)(A) – "recovery" undefined.** It is unclear whether collecting, lifting, dewatering, crushing, or at-sea processing counts as "recovery," or whether the act is complete only when minerals are brought aboard. This matters for both the tonnage count and the penalty-per-day calculation (see item 22).

5. **Sec. 2(1)(A) – 200-meter depth floor.** The threshold is tied to depth only, so nodule or crust recovery on shallower seamount summits, shelf edges, or in the 150–200 m band is outside the Act regardless of ecosystem impact.

**Sec. 2(1)(B) – Secretary's catch-all**

6. **Sec. 2(1)(B) – "the Secretary" is never defined.** The only Secretary named anywhere in the bill is the Secretary of State (Sec. 6); Sec. 4 uses NOAA, which sits under Commerce. As drafted, no one knows who has the determination authority, which makes the subparagraph unusable.

7. **Sec. 2(1)(B) – Vagueness / due-process problem.** Criminal liability (Sec. 5(b)) attaches to an open-ended "comparable risk" standard with no criteria, procedure, notice, or publication requirement. A defendant will argue void-for-vagueness; a hostile court could strike the subparagraph, and without a severability clause (item 30) that could endanger the whole Act.

8. **Sec. 2(1)(B) – Purely discretionary.** The Secretary "determines" but is never required to act, consider petitions, or respond within any timeframe. An administration that favors mining simply never makes a determination, and nothing in the bill lets a court or citizen compel one.

**Sec. 2(2) – "U.S. person"**

9. **Sec. 2(2) – Entity coverage is far too narrow.** Only "corporations" organized under the laws of "a State" are covered. Not covered: LLCs, partnerships, trusts, and other non-corporate entities; entities organized in D.C., Puerto Rico, Guam, CNMI, American Samoa, or under federal law; and lawful permanent residents and other non-citizen residents.

10. **Sec. 2(2) – Foreign subsidiaries and controlled entities escape.** A U.S. corporation can run the operation through a foreign-incorporated subsidiary it wholly owns and controls, or through a Nauru- or Tonga-sponsored affiliate, and be outside the definition entirely. Standard sanctions-style language ("any entity owned or controlled by a U.S. person") is missing.

**Sec. 2(3) – "Covered vessel"**

11. **Sec. 2(3) – 5,000-gross-ton floor and "equipped for" test.** Vessels under 5,000 GT, support vessels that tow or tend seabed collectors, and vessels that offload their mining equipment to a separate barge or platform are not "covered." Equipment can be removed while in U.S. ports and reinstalled at sea.

12. **Sec. 2(3) – Registry is disconnected from the prohibition.** "Covered vessel" is used only for Sec. 4, and Sec. 3 is written in terms of persons, not vessels. So the registry captures only large vessels, while the operations most likely to evade Sec. 3 (small-vessel fleets, item 1) also evade the registry.

**Sec. 3(a) – Prohibition**

13. **Sec. 3(a) – "in the United States" is undefined and likely excludes the EEZ and Outer Continental Shelf.** Deep seabed mining does not happen "in the United States" in the ordinary sense; it happens at sea. Unless "United States" is defined to include the territorial sea, EEZ, and OCS, a foreign person mining off Hawaii, American Samoa, or CNMI is not covered — and that is the most likely near-term U.S. mining scenario.

14. **Sec. 3(a) – "engage in" is undefined.** The prohibition reaches only whoever is "engaging" in mining, not U.S. persons who finance, insure, charter, contract for, provide vessels or technology for, or direct it. A U.S. company can contract a foreign operator and plausibly argue it is not itself "engaging."

15. **Sec. 3(a) – No downstream coverage.** Nothing prohibits importing, landing, transshipping, processing, refining, or selling seabed minerals in the United States, so the U.S. market remains fully open to foreign-mined material. The bill also does not bar federal financing (EXIM, DFC), procurement, or sponsorship support.

16. **Sec. 3(a) – U.S.-flagged vessels not covered as such.** A vessel documented in the United States but operated by a foreign LLC is outside both prongs of the prohibition. Most ocean statutes extend jurisdiction to U.S.-flag vessels regardless of operator.

17. **Sec. 3(a) – No conspiracy, attempt, or aiding-and-abetting provision.** General federal conspiracy law (18 U.S.C. § 371) may reach some criminal conduct, but nothing extends civil liability to those who assist or attempt a violation.

**Sec. 3(b) – Grandfather clause**

18. **Sec. 3(b) – Exploration licenses grandfather full-scale mining.** The exemption covers "mining" conducted under an "exploration license" — i.e., it converts every pre-enactment exploration authorization into a permanent commercial mining right. This would exempt Lockheed Martin's two DSHMRA exploration licenses (USA-1 and USA-4), any licenses NOAA issues to TMC USA or others before enactment, and arguably every ISA exploration contract held by a U.S.-linked entity. As drafted, this clause swallows the bill.

19. **Sec. 3(b) – "Issued" by anyone, anywhere, with no end date.** The clause does not say which issuer counts (NOAA, ISA, a foreign sponsoring state) and does not limit the exemption to the license's original term, area, or scope. Licenses can be renewed, extended, amended, transferred, or assigned indefinitely and remain "issued before" enactment.

20. **Sec. 3(b) – Race-to-file window.** Because the cutoff is enactment rather than introduction or committee action, the bill creates an incentive to obtain licenses between now and signing. NOAA is currently processing DSHMRA applications and could issue licenses during floor consideration.

**Sec. 3(c) – Environmental-assessment exemption**

21. **Sec. 3(c) – Unbounded "purpose" exemption.** There is no tonnage cap, duration limit, area limit, approval requirement, reporting requirement, or requirement that the assessment be for a regulator or public body. The industry already characterizes collector-system trials as environmental monitoring; an operator can recover any amount and call it an assessment.

**Sec. 4 – Registry**

22. **Sec. 4(a) – No deadline, no enforcement, no consequence.** The bill sets no registration deadline, gives NOAA no authority to deny or condition registration, and — because Sec. 5 penalties apply only to violations of Sec. 3 — attaches no penalty for failing to register. "Operator" is also undefined.

23. **Sec. 4(b) – Self-certified reports with no verification or public access.** Required contents are unspecified (no tonnage, location, depth, or method), there is no inspection, audit, recordkeeping, or observer authority, no explicit false-statement penalty, and no requirement that reports be made public. Reports are essentially voluntary narrative.

**Sec. 5 – Penalties**

24. **Sec. 5(a) – Direct conflict with Sec. 8.** Civil penalties attach to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but under Sec. 8 the prohibition is not in effect until 180 days later. Either the penalty provision is unenforceable for the first 180 days or it purports to punish lawful conduct retroactively — an easy due-process challenge and a drafting error either way.

25. **Sec. 5(a) – "Each day on which the violation occurs" does not map onto an annual tonnage threshold.** Because the offense is defined as exceeding 10,000 tons "per year," it is unclear whether the violation "occurs" only on the day the threshold is crossed, on each day thereafter, or on every day of the year retroactively. A defendant will argue for a single-day penalty.

26. **Sec. 5 – No enforcement agency, procedure, or remedies.** The bill does not say who assesses civil penalties, how (notice and hearing, judicial vs. administrative), where suit is brought, or whether courts may issue injunctions. There is no in rem forfeiture of vessels, equipment, or minerals, no citizen-suit provision, and no Coast Guard boarding or detention authority.

27. **Sec. 5(b) – "Willfully" plus a vague standard.** Willfulness is the highest federal mens rea and will be nearly impossible to prove for conduct under Sec. 2(1)(B) or near the 10,000-ton line. A "knowingly" standard, as used in the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act and most marine statutes, would be stronger.

**Sec. 6 – International agreement**

28. **Sec. 6 – Hortatory only.** "Shall seek to negotiate" imposes no obligation to report to Congress, no consequence for inaction, and is ambiguous about whether negotiations must begin or conclude within 18 months. It also says nothing about the U.S. position at the International Seabed Authority or in bilateral sponsorship arrangements.

**Sec. 7 – Duration**

29. **Sec. 7(a) and 7(b) contradict each other.** Subsection (a) says the prohibition lasts until Congress acts by joint resolution; subsection (b) says the entire Act expires in 10 years regardless. The sunset controls as the more specific provision, so the "until Congress finds" language is illusory — and the sunset also ends the registry, the penalties, and everything else.

30. **Sec. 7(b) – Sunset undermines the bill's purpose and creates a wait-it-out incentive.** A 10-year expiration measured from enactment (so only 9.5 years of actual prohibition after Sec. 8) tells investors to hold licenses and wait; combined with Sec. 3(b), grandfathered operators simply continue through the sunset.

31. **Sec. 7(a) – National Academies report is unprovided-for.** No one is directed or funded to commission the report, no scope or timeline is set, and "serious harm" is undefined. An industry-funded or narrowly scoped report could satisfy the trigger.

**Sec. 8 and general drafting gaps**

32. **Sec. 8 – 180-day delay.** The delay gives operators half a year to ramp up and stockpile, and it is the source of the Sec. 5(a) conflict (item 24). If the delay is retained, the penalty provision and the grandfather cutoff should be keyed to the same date.

33. **No severability clause.** Given the vagueness exposure in Sec. 2(1)(B) and the retroactivity problem in Sec. 5(a), a successful challenge to one provision could take down the whole Act.

34. **No relationship-to-existing-law provision.** The bill neither amends nor repeals NOAA's authority to issue commercial recovery permits under the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act (30 U.S.C. § 1401 et seq.), BOEM's OCS mineral leasing authority, or the 2025 executive order directing expedited seabed-mining permits. NOAA could continue issuing permits that the agency then argues are outside Sec. 3 or protected by Sec. 3(b).

35. **No rulemaking authority or implementing agency.** Other than naming NOAA as the registry recipient, the bill designates no agency to implement, interpret, or enforce it and grants no regulatory authority to fill the many definitional gaps above.

36. **No anti-circumvention or anti-evasion provision.** Given items 1, 2, 9, 10, 11, and 14, a general clause prohibiting structuring, splitting, or reorganizing to evade the Act would close several loopholes at once.

**If you can only fix five things before Thursday:** items 18–19 (the grandfather clause), item 13 (define "United States" to include the EEZ/OCS), item 29–30 (the sunset), item 21 (cap the environmental-assessment exemption), and item 24 (align the penalty date with the effective date). Items 6 and 33 are cheap one-line fixes that remove real litigation risk.
